channel.title: HAT MI Daily - Macro and Industries
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: Tokyo's core consumer prices, excluding fresh food, rose 2.9% year on year in November, the fastest since July 2025, after 2.6% in October, partly as government utility subsidies ended, ahead of the Bank of Japan's 18 December decision.
item.description:
The index excluding fresh food and energy rose 2.5% and overall consumer prices 2.8%, The Straits Times reports, citing the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications; Chinatimes, citing Reuters, says the core rise was slightly below the 3% expected and that Tokyo data are viewed as a leading indicator of nationwide prices. Prices also rose for food, daily necessities and hotel charges, CNA reports. Bank of Japan board member Naoki Tamura said on 26 November that the central bank must respond swiftly to signs of an inflation overshoot, including by accelerating the pace of rate rises, citing rising raw material costs including higher crude oil prices due to the Middle East conflict, CNA and The Standard report. Markets widely expect a rate rise at the meeting ending 18 December, while investors increasingly expect a lower terminal rate of 1.75%, scaling back bets on 2027 rate rises, The Economic Times reports, citing Reuters; short-term government bond yields edged higher on 27 November. The reports do not give November's national consumer price data.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

Inflation in Tokyo is rising and above the Bank of Japan's 2% target, which supports the expected December rate rise, though markets see a lower peak for rates in 2027. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, higher Japanese rates raise borrowing costs for companies and households, and the raw material costs that Tamura cites pass through to a wider range of goods. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, rising input costs in Japan may lead to further price increases along electronics, automotive and consumer goods supply chains. Points that may be worth considering include the Bank of Japan's decision on 18 December, and whether the national figures confirm Tokyo's trend.

The Straits Times | Chinatimes | CNA | CNA | The Standard | The Economic Times | The Economic Times

item.title: The Bank of England plans to cut capital requirements for the largest UK-focused banks by 60 basis points and says its review would cut major banks' requirements by about 50 basis points in normal times, adding about GBP 175 billion of lending capacity.
item.description:
The plans are backed by the Bank's Financial Policy Committee (FPC); major UK banks in aggregate would see a 30 basis point reduction, MarketScreener and The Standard report. The review found that UK-focused lenders were disproportionately affected by capital rules, and banks had raised concerns that overlapping requirements counted the same risks several times, The Standard reports. The Bank says the measures will free more capacity to lend to UK households and businesses, while the actual impact will vary with banks' business models, and the Prudential Regulation Authority will consider lower minimum requirements for domestic lending to offset keeping a 2% neutral countercyclical capital buffer rate, MarketScreener reports. Separately, Governor Andrew Bailey warned that interest rates will have to rise further if energy prices remain elevated, with inflation at 3.6%, The Daily Mail reports. The reports do not give a timetable for the changes.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The Bank of England plans to loosen bank capital rules while its governor warns that interest rates will have to rise further if energy prices remain elevated, so the amount of credit banks can supply and its cost may move in different directions. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, more lending capacity matters most for smaller firms and housing finance, while the price of credit is still set by the policy rate. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, easier bank lending could support UK construction and smaller manufacturing customers if it is not offset by higher rates. Points that may be worth considering include when the changes take effect, and the Bank of England's rate decision in December.

MarketScreener | The Standard | The Standard | MarketScreener | The Daily Mail

item.title: Yemen's Houthis said on 25 November that they had attacked Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery and a financial centre in Riyadh, claiming a direct hit and fires at the refinery, and threatened further attacks on the kingdom.
item.description:
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree claimed that the strike on the refinery in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province was "direct" and caused "fires at the facility", and said the second operation targeted a financial centre in Riyadh in three stages, Daily Times reports. He vowed that the group would continue its military operations against Saudi Arabia. The report gives no Saudi confirmation, no damage assessment, and no effect on refinery output or exports.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

This is a claim by one side of the conflict, reported by one outlet, with no confirmation of damage. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, Ras Tanura is one of Saudi Arabia's main refining and export sites, so a confirmed disruption there would matter for oil and product supply; without confirmation, the main effect is on the perceived risk to Gulf energy infrastructure. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, oil and refined products feed petrochemical raw materials such as solvents and monomers, so attacks on Gulf refining add to input-cost risk. Points that may be worth considering include whether Saudi Arabia confirms damage or output losses, and whether attacks extend to other export facilities.

Daily Times

item.title: EU leaders ended their special summit on the 2028–2034 long-term budget early without agreement, with Chancellor Merz saying views on its size and distribution remain far apart and the total of EUR 1.78 trillion too high.
item.description:
Council President António Costa had scheduled the summit for two days to make headway on the next long-term budget, Handelsblatt reports. Merz, with the group of the "Sensible Seven", insists on a strict course of austerity; despite the cuts recently proposed by Costa, the total of EUR 1.78 trillion is too high, he said at the start of the summit, Handelsblatt and Süddeutsche Zeitung report. He said the latest compromise proposal was not a basis for concluding negotiations and called for priority on spending for a competitive economy and better defence capabilities, Handelsblatt reports. Germany wants the framework to allow further loans to Ukraine by qualified majority, while Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic continue to reject joint financing, Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung reports; most leaders want to find a solution for the budget and Ukraine on 17 December. If a further summit in December also brings no result, France has threatened that negotiations would not continue until after the French presidential election scheduled for April, Handelsblatt reports. The reports do not give the size of the gap between the camps or the spending lines in dispute.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The EU has not agreed its 2028–2034 budget, and the next attempt is in December, with France threatening a pause until after April if that fails. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, the long-term budget sets the size of EU programmes for cohesion, research, industry and defence, so a later agreement delays new programmes and the projects they fund. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, EU-funded construction, infrastructure and industrial projects are a source of demand in several member states, and a priority for competitiveness and defence would shape which sectors gain. Points that may be worth considering include the outcome of the 17 December meeting, and whether the budget is linked to Ukraine financing in the final deal.

Handelsblatt | Handelsblatt | Handelsblatt | Süddeutsche Zeitung | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung

item.title: Chinese electric vehicle makers' sales exceeded those of Japanese competitors in 39 markets in January–September 2026, 14 more markets than a year earlier, though not in the US or Japan, Challenges reports.
item.description:
Chinese manufacturers are supplanting Toyota, Honda and other Japanese carmakers market after market in Asia and Europe, Challenges writes, adding that the electric vehicle sector has been strengthened by the Strait of Hormuz crisis, which raised oil prices and made combustion-engine vehicles more expensive to use. Electric vehicles took 16% of global vehicle sales in 2025, according to the International Energy Agency, cited by Challenges. Chinese carmakers have announced a series of industrial investments in Europe in recent months, including BYD's takeover of the Ineos site in Hambach, Moselle, Les Echos reports, while Chinese manufacturers export mainly to find an outlet for excess factory capacity. The reports do not give sales volumes, the list of the 39 markets, or whether the Japanese figures cover electric models only.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The comparison is a count of markets, not a measure of volume or market share, but it shows Chinese makers overtaking Japanese brands in a growing number of markets. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a shift of share between brands changes where vehicles are built and which supply chains serve them, since Chinese makers mostly export from China while adding some plants abroad. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, this moves demand for battery, electronics and body bonding towards Chinese carmakers and their suppliers, at home and in their new foreign plants, and away from the supply base of Japanese makers in the markets they lose. Points that may be worth considering include where Chinese makers place new plants, and whether Japanese makers' electrified models recover share.

Challenges | Les Echos

item.title: UK vehicle production rose 4.8% year on year in October to 64,141 units, with car output up 6.2% for a third monthly rise, and car exports up 14.2%, including 70.9% more to the US and 7.1% less to the EU, SMMT data show.
item.description:
Car production reached 61,746 units, and exports took 82.6% of it, the highest monthly proportion since December 2024, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) figures reported by MarketScreener; shipments to the EU account for more than half of car exports. The reports do not give commercial vehicle output separately, year-to-date production, or the share of electric models in output.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

UK car output rose for a third consecutive month, and car exports grew 14.2%, with a sharp rise in shipments to the US and a fall in shipments to the EU, the largest destination. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, about 62,000 cars a month is small against the major European producers, and one month's rise in exports to one market can reflect model launches or shipping timing. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, higher car output supports demand for body, interior and electronics bonding at UK plants and their suppliers. Points that may be worth considering include whether the rise in US-bound exports continues, and whether exports to the EU recover.

MarketScreener | MarketScreener

item.title: China's State Council executive meeting has adopted the 15th Five-Year Plan for urban renewal, under which about 770,000 km of urban underground pipeline networks are to be built or renovated, with total investment exceeding CNY 5 trillion.
item.description:
On 12 November, a matchmaking meeting in Nanjing on the investment, construction and operation of the "Six Networks" promoted 196 projects with total investment of CNY 379.78 billion, with underground pipeline network projects first at 63 projects, Xhby reports. China's urban underground pipeline network is about 3.9 million km long, the largest in the world, according to the report. The report does not give the date of the State Council meeting, the split of investment between new and renovated networks, a yearly spending profile, or funding sources.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The plan sets a national length target and an investment total for one type of urban infrastructure over the five-year period, but a plan is not yet activity and the report gives no yearly spending profile. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, pipeline renewal is spread over many cities and years, which tends to give steadier demand than single large projects. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, pipe joining, repair and protection use sealing and bonding materials, so a programme of this size could add to demand in China's infrastructure segment. Points that may be worth considering include how much of the investment is funded in 2027, and whether local government finances allow the pace the plan sets.

Xhby

item.title: Germany's GfK consumer climate index rose to minus 30.2 for December from minus 30.9 for November, as expected, with income expectations and willingness to buy up slightly, but economic expectations fell and inflation concerns rose.
item.description:
The value was in line with the forecast of economists polled by The Wall Street Journal, and consumer sentiment is slightly lower than a year earlier, according to the Nuremberg Institute for Market Decisions and GfK data reported by MarketScreener. Economic expectations had risen for six consecutive months before this decline. Separately, Jörg Dittrich, president of the Central Association of German Crafts (ZDH), warned of a "silent dying of businesses" if politicians do not take counteractive measures soon, saying up to 80,000 jobs a year are threatened, over 150,000 have been lost in the past two years, and the crafts business climate is at the level of the COVID-19 pandemic, Handelsblatt reports. DIW president Marcel Fratzscher said Germany must prepare for two more very difficult years with President Donald Trump in the White House, and that new tariffs create uncertainty, though he forecast growth of more than 1% for 2027, The Straits Times reports. The reports do not give the sub-index levels or the size of the year-on-year difference in the consumer climate.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

German consumer sentiment remains deeply negative and almost unchanged, with slightly higher income expectations and willingness to buy nudging the index up, while economic expectations fell and inflation concerns rose, while the crafts association describes its business climate as at pandemic level. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a consumer climate this low points to restrained spending on durable goods, furnishing and renovation, and the crafts warning points the same way for small building and repair firms. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, weak consumer demand in Germany weighs on DIY, renovation and consumer durables, which use flooring, tile, sealing and assembly adhesives. Points that may be worth considering include whether income expectations keep rising in the next readings, and whether inflation concerns ease.

MarketScreener | Handelsblatt | The Straits Times

item.title: Two out of three automotive suppliers and medium-sized trailer, body and bus makers surveyed by VDA are postponing, relocating or cancelling investments planned for Germany, and more than half are cutting jobs in Germany.
item.description:
The survey by the German Association of the Automotive Industry (VDA) covered automotive suppliers (Manufacturer Group III) and medium-sized manufacturers of trailers, vehicle bodies and buses (Manufacturer Group II), VDA says. Among the companies cutting jobs in Germany, 43% are creating positions abroad at the same time. The release does not give the number of companies surveyed, the survey period, the size of the investments concerned, or the countries that receive relocated investments.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The survey shows that two out of three surveyed suppliers and medium-sized trailer, body and bus makers are holding back on investment in Germany, and that 43% of the companies cutting jobs in Germany are creating positions abroad at the same time. The figures are shares of the companies surveyed, not amounts of investment or numbers of jobs. On a general reading rather than on anything in the source, supplier investment decisions set where component production sits for years, so postponed or relocated projects reduce the German production base before vehicle output itself shows it. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, makers of interiors, electronics, bodies and battery components use bonding and sealing materials, so a shift of their production abroad would move part of that demand out of Germany rather than remove it. Points that may be worth considering include which countries receive the relocated investments, and whether vehicle makers' own investment plans in Germany follow the same pattern.

VDA

item.title: India's Supreme Court has ordered separate front-of-pack warning labels for high salt, sugar and fat on packaged food, tightening a government plan for a single label, with rules due within four months and 365 days for packaging changes.
item.description:
On 26 November, the court rejected a proposal to club all three nutrients under one symbol: each must be identified by a separate hexagon carrying the words "High Fat", "High Sugar" or "High Salt" with a matching pictogram, The Times of India reports. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has been asked to bring the rules into force within four months, in line with the timeline it had proposed, and food companies will then have 365 days to make the changes to their packaging. Business Standard and MarketScreener describe the ruling as a blow to the USD 100 billion food and drinks industry, which has long opposed the measure, and name PepsiCo, Mondelez, Coca-Cola and Nestlé among the players that opposed such labels; The Statesman says these companies are likely to face greater compliance requirements. The government's plan for front-of-pack red warning labels came after heated public debate on the lack of such measures, Business Standard reports. The reports do not give the number of products affected, rules on label size or placement, or how imported products will be treated.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

This is a court-ordered labelling change for packaged food sold in India, with a timetable: rules within four months and then a year for packaging changes. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a mandatory change to the front of a pack leads to the redesign and reprinting of labels and packaging across whole product ranges within a fixed window, which concentrates converting and printing work in that period. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, label and flexible-packaging conversion uses laminating and label adhesives, so a nationwide relabelling in a large food market could raise demand from converters and printers in India for a limited time. Points that may be worth considering include the final FSSAI rules on label format and placement, and whether other markets in the region adopt similar warning labels.

The Times of India | Business Standard | MarketScreener | The Statesman
